answer.rationale: Timeline points at the release: deploy 2h ago, degradation began 90m ago, so the release is the leading candidate cause even though the 30-minute gap means correlation is not proof. memory_b2 explicitly rules out regional_failover here 	hat is the exact condition it warns against, writes hot at settlement peak, and the 40-minute replication gap already cost writes once; that directly violates the 'without losing customer writes' objective. add_capacity (memory_b3) worked for a demand surge with flat queue depth; this is a rising-latency-after-change pattern, not a demand surge, so it would likely mask rather than fix. enable_circuit_breaker (memory_b4) treats an external dependency failure, which is not indicated. route_read_replicas (memory_b5) helped when read load from dashboards was crowding the primary; nothing suggests read pressure here. That leaves rollback. I verify memory_b1 because it is the record I am actually acting on and its claim of 'no customer impact' is the load-bearing assumption \I need the original to know whether that rollback was reversing a code-only change or one with schema/data migration, since reversing a migration under hot settlement writes is precisely how a rollback could lose writes. I verify memory_b6 because it establishes whether staged/canary gating exists on this path; if it does, I can roll back one cohort and read the write-path p99 signal before committing everywhere, which is why I am scoping this as a small guarded test rather than a broad rollout. Risk flagged: b1 was consolidated at day 18 and both records are summaries whose caveats may have been compressed out the way b2's nearly was; if b1 turns out to involve migration reversal, or if no cohort gating exists, I hold the rollback for the next window rather than spend my single intervention on an unbounded write-risk action. Guarded rollback also keeps the release-as-cause hypothesis falsifiable: if cohort p99 does not recover, cause is elsewhere and I have not burned the blast radius.
